harris-west-point-1895-08.A1:
A FATHER'S HIGH HONOR
AS AN OFFICER HE PROTECTS THE ASSAULTER OF HIS OWN CHILD.
The Brute Paid the Penalty of His Crime on the Scaffold in King and Queen County-He Confessed His Guilt.
The negro Harris, who was a short time ago charged with an attempt to commit criminal assault upon a six-year-old white child in King and Queen county, and sentenced to be hanged, was executed to-day at King and Queen Courthouse in privacy.

A large crowd assembled to view the scene, but only thirty-four people were permitted to see him hung.

At about 12 o'clock the prisoner was led to the scaffold, where he announced to the public that he had sinned, and warned the people in his hearing to take a lesson from his example. He said he felt that God had pardoned him, and was ready to meet death.

At 10 minutes past 12 P. M., the trapdoor dropped, and he was pronounced dead by a physician present in twelve minutes afterwards.

He was taken down and buried near the court-house.

The crime was a remarkable one in many respects. While the negro failed of his purpose, his guilt was undoubted. The matter was reported to the father of the child by two sons older than the girl, after the negro had offered to pay them not to tell, and also threatened to kill them both if either said a word about the crime.

The father was a deputy-sheriff and also the jailer of the county. He himself made the arrest, and while on the way to the jail with his prisoner, was forced to protect him from the threatened violence of a mob, who desired to weak speed vengeance upon the brute.

The jailer is an old Confederate soldier, and it is a fact worthy of note that he had the high sense of the duties of his office under such extraordinary circumstances to protect the villain who sought to ruin his own child. He warded off the would-be lynchers, and told them that, as an officer of the law, it was his duty to see that the law took its course.
Harris was nineteen years old and committed the crime when the jailer and his wife were away from home.

The Negro Youth Harris Hanged at King and Queen Courthouse.

He was attended by Rev. Charles Morris, who read a few verses of Scripture and offered a short, impressive, and appropriate prayer. When Harris was asked if he had any statement to make he did not refer to his crime, but urged all who heard him to take warning from his end and prepare to meet God. He expressed himself as ready to die and at peace with God. The rope was adjusted and the black cap placed over his head, and at 12:10 the trap was sprung by Sheriff Eubank. The drop was about five feet. In fifteen minutes Harris was pronounced dead by the attending physicians. Drs. Garrett and Flauntleroy.

Harris's crime was committed early in July last.

HIS ACCOUNT OF HIMSELF.

Harris's account of himself was that he was born in Richmond in 1873, and attended the public schools (Moore street and Baker street) for five years. He said he was a newspaper carrier for Jackson Ward for three years, and that in 1891 he drove a delivery wagon for a grocer. He came to this county in July, 1892 on a visit, and was so taken with
Jackson ward for three years, and that in 1891 he drove a delivery wagon for a grocer. He came to this county in July, 1892, on a visit, and was so taken with country life that he never went back to his home. He was a member of Bethlehem Baptist church, a teacher in the Sunday school, and a rising light in the church.

One of the remarkable features of the case is that the boy never heard, directly, a word from any of his relatives, although he wrote a number of letters to them. Mr. Oliver, the jailer, received a letter from one John Wallace, who the boy said was his uncle, and a huckster in the Second Market, making inquiries about the boy. Wallace wrote that he had received a letter purporting to be from the boy, but that he considered it a hoax. The boy said his father was a porter on a Pullman-car between Augusta, Ga., and New York, on the Atlantic-Coast Line, and that his name was Robert Henry Harris.

harris-west-point-1895-08.A8:
MORE THAN ROMAN VIRTUE.
The Atlanta Constitution pays a deserved tribute to a Virginia public officer when it says "Roman virtue is a rare thing in our day, but this Virginian seems to have it."

The incident that called for this high praise is given in a few short paragraphs:

At West Point, Va., the other day a negro was hanged for attempting to feloniously assault a six year-old white girl.

We have no hesitation in declaring it the most remarkable case that ever occurred in this country, or perhaps in any other.

The negro's guilt was undoubted. He offered to pay the girl's two older brothers if they would not report his crime, which they had discovered, to their father, but the two boys made the facts known.

Then the father, who is a deputy sheriff, and also jailor of the county, made the arrest, and on his way to the jail protected the prisoner from the threatened violence of the mob. The Richmond Dispatch states that this singular father is an old Confederate soldier, and says that he must have had a high sense of honor and duty under such extraordinary circumstances to protect the villain who had sought to ruin his child. He warded off the would-be lynchers, and told them that as an officer of the law it was his duty to see that the law took it course.

We read of such stern devotion to public duty among the old Romans, but never before was such an instance recorded in our annals. It would be interesting to know more about the personality of this wonderful deputy sheriff.

Killed by a Negro.
Killed by a Negro.
Luling, Texas, August 12.—A desperate shooting affray took place yesterday evening at Martindale, eighteen miles west of here, in which a young white man named Henry Hightower, was shot and instantly killed by a negro named Henry Wade. Saturday evening Wade and a brother-in-law of Hightower's had a difficulty and the negro knocked the white man in the head with a rock, badly injuring him. Yesterday evening Hightower met the negro near the Baptist church, in the edge of town, and fired on him twice with a pistol. The negro replied with a shotgun. Wade was captured and carried to jail at Lockhart.
henry-wade-lockhart-1895-08-16.A2:
A Lynching Frustrated.
Luling, Texas, August 15.—It is learned here that an attempt was made to lynch Henry Wade, the negro who killed Henry Hightower at Martindale Sunday night and that it was frustrated by the negro making a race for the officers under whose protection he placed himself. The negro is now in jail at Seguin.

james-stockton-broad-ripple-1895-08-07.A2:
ASSASSIN RUN TO EARTH.
Boy Follows a Dog into a Barn and Is
Fired Upon.
Indianapolis, Aug. 8—Barney Cline Is
Indianapolis, Aug. 8.—Barney Cline is a wealthy farmer of Washington township, this county. A strange dog was noticed yesterday lurking about the barn, and Ernest Cline, a grandson, undertook to investigate. He followed the dog into the barn and as he opened the door he was fired upon from the inside, a load of buckshot carrying away his hat, while his face wa badly burned by the flash of powder. The would-be assassin escaped.

The neighborhood was aroused and a mob of men and boys, heavily armed and re-enforced by dogs, followed in chase, which lasted the entire night. This afternoon the assassin was captured near Broad Ripple. He proved to be James Stockton, colored, who recently came from Kentucky. The older citizens had difficulty in preventing a lynching. The Cline family are unable to account for the assault, and the negro offers no explanation.

lockhardt-racine-1895-08-09.A1:
RACE WAR AT RACINE.
Street Laborers Engage in a Freefor-all Fight-Objected to a Colored Boss.
Racine, Wis., Aug. 9.—[Special.]

There was a great deal of excitement on one of the principal streets this morning and for a time there threatened to be serious trouble between the city laborers. It was nothing less than a race war and the whites were pitted against the blacks. Contractor Jones recently brought a colored man from Milwaukee named Lockhardt to supervise the street work. He appeared to be a very tyrannical sort of a fellow and the people in the vicinity of where the men were at work made complaint about the manner in which he treated the laborers.

This morning he discharged a man named George Sherry. The latter refused to quit work until he had received his money. Lockhardt told him to see the contractor and get his dues. Shortly afterwards the colored boss was walking along the street when he was attacked by Sherry. A general fight ensued and the white man got the worst of it. Some white men who were near at hand started to take sides with Sherry when the whole force of colored men joined sides with Lockhardt and there was a fight on all sides for a time. The colored men had the best of the encounter as they were in the majority, but when the police appeared on the scene they dispersed.

Lockhardt was arrested and placed in jail, but afterwards released on bonds. More trouble is threatened, as the white men are thoroughly aroused.

tom-johnson-hattiesburg-1895-07-26.A1:
LYNCH LAW IN MISSISSIPPI.
A Negro Charged With Murder May
be Born At the Age of 18.
Meridian, Miss., July 26.—Tom Johnson, the negro who, it is alleged, murdered Mrs. Hartfield and her daughter and assaulted her other daughter at Hattiesburg, was captured at Ellisville and carried back to Hattiesburg and placed in jail. Last night a crowd of citizens went to the jail and demanded the prisoner; upon being refused by the sheriff they knocked a hole through the wall and broke open about seven locks before reaching the negro's cell.

When the mob arrived at his door he showed fight, having secured a crowbar, and had to be shot several times before the mob could secure him. He was carried out to the scene of his crime, which is about 14 miles from Hattiesburg, for identification; and if he proves that to be the right party it is certain that he will be lynched, and there is talk of burning him at the stake.
tom-johnson-hattiesburg-1895-07-26.A3: Tom Johnson, the negro who murdered Katie Hartfield, wounded and ravished her sister, and almost killed Mrs. Hartfield, was captured, carried to the scene of his crime, carried to the scene of his crime, and shot to death by a force of 500 or more men last Saturday evening. There was no effort at concealment, and after after Johnson's confession he was allowed to select his own mode of death.
tom-johnson-hattiesburg-1895-07-26.A6:
HORRIBLE!
A Negro Fiend Knocks Two Young Ladies in the Head With a Hatchet.
Assaults one of the Girls and Shoots the Mother.
With a Hatchet.

Assaults one of the Girls and Shoots the Mother.

On Saturday night, July 20th, at about 9 o'clock, near Hattiesburg another fearful crime was committed by a negro brute by the name of Tom Johnson. On the night in question the daughters of Mr. A. D. Hartfield, Misses Katie and Susie Hartfield, aged 14 and 16 years, respectively, had occasion to go to the barn, and had stepped out of the house into the lot and were met by a negro, who struck Katie over the head with an ax, splitting her head wide open. Her sister, Miss Susie, seeing her fate, cried for help. At this the negro turned to her and dealt, as he supposed, a death blow, and dragged her to a crib, a distance of fifty yards and outraged her leaving her for dead.

The mother of the girls went to the lot in search of them and was met at the gate by the negro, who began firing at her with a 38-caliber revolver, hitting her three times, though not fatally.

Mrs. Hartfield wounded and bleeding fled to the house, the negro followed whereupon she left the house and hid under it, the negro thinking the coast clear ransacked trunks and whatever place he thought articles of value or money were concealed. In the meantime Mrs. Hartfield fled to a neighbor's house about a mile distant and gave the alarm, and a body of neighbors returned only to find that the flendish wretch had escaped, leaving his innocent victims dabbled in blood, in the cow pen, one of whom has since died. The neighbors at once raised the alarm, and the news of the revolting crime spread like wild fire to the adjoining counties and large
Mr. Hartfield had given a description. About sundown he was observed by Mr. Reddoch and his son and nephew. The first named is an aged man and the two youths mere strippling, but proved to be heroes. The negro, whom they recognized as the hunted fugive, was on the road leading to Reddoch's ferry, and on inquiry as to where he could stay all night was directed to a negro cabin near by. The man and boys formed a plan to capture him, and sent for help, but fearing he would escape before aid arrived boldly approached the cabin, and there beheld the execrable wretch, whose hands not long since was freshly dyed with the blood of innocent human beings, uplifted and leading in prayer the other negroes of the place. Oh, what a despicable and hypocritical scoundrel.

Mr. Reddoch and the two young men entered the cabin, and drawing their pistols ordered him to hold up his hands and surrender. He hesitated, and suddenly made a move towards his trouser's pockets, but as he did so one of the party pulled the trigger. The cartridge failed to explode, but it had the desired effect and the negro gave up and his captors conveyed him to the county jail at Hattiesburg, where the indignant people gathered and broke open the prison, and artor a desperate resistance, was finally subdued, and the crowd started with him to the Hartfield home to be identified, but on the road he made his escape, and after a long chase was re-captured and carried before Mrs. Hartfield, who fully identified Johnson as the negro who committed the crimes mentioned. Then measures were taken for his execution. A committee was appointed, and after making a confession, he was allowed to choose his own manner of death. Johnson desired to be shoot, and accordingly he was tied between two saplings and over one thousand shots fired into his body, and all that remained of Tom Johnson, the murderer
"I left Meridian Tuesday night, July 16, 1895, and came down to Hattiesburg and went out to Mrs. E. M. Summerall's and attempted to rob her house on the Wednesday night following, firing the field fence first. I immediately went down to Mr. W. J. Draughan's, firing his field fence first and then robbed his house. No one was with me. I carried out of Mr. Draughan's house a trunk and then went back and carried out another trunk. I went to Mr. A. D. Hartfield's on Saturday night, the 20th, and hit his daughter Susie with an ax and knocked her down. I then knocked his daughter Katie down with the ax and killed her. I hit her two licks with the ax. Mrs. Hartfield came running up and I shot her twice with my pistol. I shot at the dog once, and followed it to the house. I then went into the house to rob it, but did not find any money. I then went back to the lot where Susie was knocked down and took her up and put her in the crib. I did all this myself. No one was with me and no one had any knowledge of my being in the country.
I know nothing of the killing of Mrs. Williamson in Hattiesburg, nor of the Farmer family in Meridian. I brought a cake of bread with me from Neshoba county when I came to this county, and lived on it and peaches and watermelons until I committed the crime at A. D. Hartfield's. I feel that I ought to die for these crimes. Signed by me this 20th day of July.

In response to requests from the U. S. Consul at Panama and the New York officers of the Panama railroad, Secretary Herbert has ordered a ship to Panama. There are two sources from which trouble is feared. There is a labor strike now on hand, and Ecuador is said to be about to invade Colombia, which gives the United States the right to maintain free communication over the Panama railroad whenever Colombia fails to do so. Of course Secretary Herbert's instructions have not been made public, but it is almost certain that they include keeping of the Panama railroad open, as well as protecting American interests in general.

I desire to correct one of the malicious reports in circulation concerning me in all counties that I have visited and perhaps throughout the entire state: that I am seventy-six years of age, and therefore too old to run for the office. tom-johnson-hattiesburg-1895-07-26.A12:
WAS NOT BURNED,
But Literally Riddled with Bullets for His Crime.
NEW ORLEANS July 97 - A special to
NEW ORLEANS, July 27.—A special to the Daily States from Hattiesburg, Miss, says:
The negro, Tom Johnson, after being taken from jail at this place Wednesday night by a mob of 100 men, made his escape, reaching the Hartsfield residence. The entire day Thursday was devoted to his capture, which occurred at 4 o'clock in the evening.
The men, who were completely worn out for lack of sleep and rest, spent the night with their prisoner within three miles of Hattiesburg, and at 6 o'clock yesterday morning started with him for the Hartsfield place, which was reached at 10 o'clock. He was taken before the wounded woman, and after being identified, made a confession. He was then taken out in the woods, and, in the presence of an immense crowd, at 2 o'clock yesterday afternoon, his body was riddled with bullets. He implicated no one else, saying he alone committed the deed.
tom-johnson-hattiesburg-1895-07-26.A14:
THE MISSISSIPPI LYNCHING.
Tom Johnson Makes Full Confession Before Being Shot.
Jackson, Miss., July 27.—A dispatch received this afternoon from Hattiesburg, Miss., gives further particulars of the crime and chase after Tom Johnson, an ex-convict, which resulted in his lynching at that place yesterday afternoon. Johnson made an assault upon Mrs. Hartfield and her two daughters at her home sixteen miles Southwest of Hattiesburg, which resulted in the death of the younger daughter and the wounding of Mrs. Hartfield and the older daughter. After committing the crime Johnson made his escape and was soon followed by an infuriated mob, the chase covering a territory of 100 miles or more. Johnson was firally captured in Covington county and taken to Hattiesburg and confined in jail there. After being recaptured Johnson was bound hand and foot and the march to the Hartfield residence was resumed. Before reaching the place, however, it was decided to stop and spend the remainder of the night, in order that the men might get some rest. A strong guard was placed over Johnson. ABOUT OUR PEOPLE.
charlotteville, Aug. 2—The scholars of Colored Public Schools of the Division taught by Mr. Robert Kelser and Mr. John A. Brown entertained the White Normal School which has been in session here for the past three weeks, by a concert and exhibition at the First Colored Church Monday after noon.

Tom Johnson of H attiesburg Miss. was taken from jail by a mob. He escaped but was recaptured. He was then taken before the wounded woman and after being indentified made a full confession. He was taken to the woods and in the presence of an immense crowd his body was riddled with buck shot.

The honor of Victoria Cross has for the first time in the history of that order been conferred upon a colored man—a coal-black negro who saved the life of his superior on the field of battle by throwing himself in front of his commander and receiving in his own body the bullets that would otherwise have struck his chief. The dark skin-ned hero is a corporal in one of the West India reigments of the British army.

London, July 30—M. D. Conway has presented to the anti lynchig committee the report of his recent visit to America. He says in his report that he does not doubt that the agitation of Mrs. Ida B. Wells Barnett and the formation of the English committee has had a good effect in America, the or me having nearly disappeared in some of the southern states, where no suggestion is now heard of the Negro propensity for assault. He finds, he says, that there is much intense feeling in the south against lynching and he believes that some great protest will presently arise in that region.

One of the most cowardly and diabolical murders that ever disgraced our city occurred on Friday 19th inst. A white thug named Mitchell, who had previously murdered three men in cold blood, met Mr. Max Mullen, one of the most peaceable and law-abiding citizens of this community, and in broad daylight, about 5 o'clock, while on his way home from his day's labor, plunged a knife into his heart, killing him instantly without cause or provocation. We are opposed to lynch law in every form except in a case of this sort and even now we would hesitate, but for the fact, that this self-same murderer seemed to have such a pull somewhere that he has been permitted to walk our streets freely, until he met Mr. Mullen on the street at a time when the fire of hell was burning within him, when his heart was steeped in a flow of malice as black and damning as it was possible to be; he like the coward he was, without warning, sent the good man into eternity. We repeat that even in this case we would be willing to let the law take its course, but when we see how tardy the courts have been, how this very murderer has committed mur er after murder with impunity, and instead of being in the penitentiary or on the hangman's scaffold, he is lorded and courted for his political pull, we are forced to ask the people of New Orleans how long will this much imposed upon community remain silent.—New Orleans; La

THE TALK OF THE DAY.
A Bridgeport inventor says he has discovered an explosive which will blow an invading army into cats' meat as soon as it is dropped among them. He has gone to Cuba to try it upon General Campos and his peninsular myrmidons, and if news from that island were not so habitually untrustworthy, it would now be awaited with increased interest. So many destructive agents of warfare are reported in this period that if all their claims were realized war would become impossible, and another mode of settling internecine and international difficulties would have to be devised. But many of them thunder in the index, exploding with more smoke than carnage, and effecting no revolutionary change in military methods. The Bridgeport fulminant may be in this category, but its pretensions remain to be tested, and inspire no great confidence.

There is an educated horse in Nashville that would be a valuable acquisition to a tented aggregation of equestrian prodigies. In one respect this horse is superior to the people of Memphis, in that it knows Nashville's ways and humors. The owner of the animal evidently reposes the most perfect confidence in it, for, without bridle or reins, he drives through the most crowded thoroughfares, guiding the horse by word of mouth, occasionally putting emphasis upon his orders by using the whip. Those who saw the intelligent steer going up Vine-st. the other afternoon at a lively pace without either bridle or lines, congratulated themselves that they were on the sidewalk rather than in the buggy it was drawing.—(Nashville American.

In Hattiesburg, Miss., of late, a lynching party waited upon one Johnson, a negro, who had in some way inflicted a wound upon its moral sensibilities, and politely gave him the privilege of selecting the mode in which he would rather be slain. They were prepared to burn, hang or shoot him, but recognized his right and were generously willing to concede to him the privilege of choosing between them. He chose the latter, and the local journal extols the neat manner in which the job was done, and the fine politeness which accompanied all its stages. Upward of five hundred shots were fired at the victim, and it is recited with pride that most of them live, and that the marksmanship did credit to the region. It is some weeks since Mississippi had previously been heard from in this way, but she comes to the front again with an uncommonly fine display of ceremony. But outside of her own borders there is little admiration for the incident and not much for the grade of civilization which she habitually evinces.

In one of the recent public-school examinations in this city the pupils were directed to write what they knew about Columbus. One little boy handed in the following: "Christopher Columbus was born in 1492. In 1776 he wandered off into the woods with a hatchet, and was never heard of again."

Both Equal to the Occasion.—A well-to-do gentleman of middle age said to me several days ago: "Do you know that I had rather shell green peas than do almost anything else? My wife says that it demoralizes the servants to have me do it, but I'm not living for the servants.

"The other day I sat down on our back porch with a pan of my favorite vegetables in my lap, and was enjoying myself in great shape, far from the madding crowd, for my wife had some swell callers.

"All of a sudden I heard a woman's voice say:

"Oh, I must see your cute back yard; I've heard so much of it."

"Then the window flew open and out popped two pretty bonneted heads.

"I turned mine away, and my wife was equal to the occasion.

"Patrick,' she said, 'you must remember to mow that grass before Mr. —— comes home."

"Yis, ma'am,' I replied in my best brogue, and all was well."—(Louisville Post.
